books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Rutherford B. Hayes Presidential Library & Museums, “Frequently Asked Questions on the 1876 Election”

stimulus.text:
| 1876 presidential election | Samuel J. Tilden (Democrat) | Rutherford B. Hayes (Republican) |
| Popular vote | 4,288,546 | 4,034,311 |
| Electoral votes, first count | 184 | 165 |

Twenty electoral votes were disputed: Florida (4), Louisiana (8), South Carolina (7), and one from Oregon. A candidate needed 185 electoral votes to win.

stem: The Compromise of 1877 ended Reconstruction. Its most direct result in the South was that

options.text: the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments were repealed.
options.misconception: Background: the amendments stayed in the Constitution; they were simply no longer enforced in the South.

options.text: Black men lost the right to vote under federal law.
options.misconception: Background: the Fifteenth Amendment still stood; Southern states limited the vote with other rules instead.

options.text: federal troops left, and Democratic “Redeemer” governments took full control.
the Freedmen’s Bureau reopened its schools.
options.misconception: Background: the Bureau had closed in 1872, five years earlier.

rationales.A: Background: the amendments stayed in the Constitution; they were simply no longer enforced in the South.
rationales.B: Background: the Fifteenth Amendment still stood; Southern states limited the vote with other rules instead.
rationales.C: The bargain’s price was the withdrawal of the last federal troops from South Carolina and Louisiana. With the soldiers gone, Democratic governments that called themselves Redeemers ruled the South without federal interference.
rationales.D: Background: the Freedmen’s Bureau had closed in 1872, five years earlier.
rationales.general:
1. The disputed votes in the table all came from states where federal troops still guarded Republican governments.
2. The bargain gave Hayes those votes, and Hayes gave the Democrats what they wanted in return.
3. What they wanted was the troops gone and their own governments in charge.
4. By the spring of 1877, the last soldiers had left and the Redeemers ruled alone.
Remember: Reconstruction was enforced by soldiers, so removing the soldiers removed Reconstruction.
